case_name: Anjani Technoplast Ltd. v. Shubh Gautam
holding_summary: The Supreme Court set aside admission of a Section 7 IBC petition filed by a decree-holder against a solvent, functioning company, holding that a decree-holder with the full machinery of civil execution available cannot invoke insolvency jurisdiction as a substitute for execution proceedings. The Court also found the decree-holder had taken contradictory positions on the debt quantum across different forums (income-tax proceedings versus the civil suit), and restored the NCLT's order dismissing the Section 7 application while imposing costs of Rs. 5 lakh.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that the IBC is a reorganisation-and-revival mechanism, not a recovery tool, and gives corporate debtors a stronger footing to resist Section 7 applications filed by decree-holders who have not exhausted execution remedies.

case_name: Sandeep S. Ghandat & Ors. v. Reserve Bank of India & Ors.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that RBI's power under Section 36AAA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to supersede the board of a multi-State co-operative bank is not circumscribed by the six-month cap on supersession of elected bodies under Article 243ZL(1) of the Constitution. The Court upheld continued supersession of the Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank board beyond its original tenure, subject to the statutory outer limit of five years, and held that consultation with the concerned State government is not a precondition.
why_it_matters: Confirms RBI has a wide, largely unfettered hand to keep a multi-State co-operative bank's board superseded during a prolonged resolution process, which is significant for depositors, bank management, and any party litigating governance disputes at troubled co-operative banks.

case_name: Fresenius Kabi Ipsum Srl v. The Assistant Controller of Patents and Designs
citation: Delhi High Court, order dated 31 August 2026
holding_summary: The Delhi High Court held that examination hearings under Section 14 of the Patents Act and pre-grant opposition hearings under Section 25(1) are distinct, parallel processes that do not converge, and that a pre-grant opposition hearing cannot substitute an applicant's separate statutory right to a Section 14 hearing. Justice Jyoti Singh set aside the refusal of Fresenius Kabi's process patent application for sugammadex (originally filed in 2016) purely on this procedural ground, without going into the merits of patentability.
why_it_matters: Patent applicants facing a refusal issued only after a pre-grant opposition hearing now have a clear procedural ground to challenge that refusal if they were never separately heard under Section 14 - a recurring gap in Patent Office practice.

case_name: A.K. Ghosh & Company and Others v. Biman Bose and Others
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that the mandatory 120-day outer limit under Order VIII Rule 1 CPC (as modified for commercial suits) applies not only to a defendant's written statement but equally to a plaintiff's written statement filed in answer to a defendant's counter-claim. The plaintiffs' attempt to file their reply to the counter-claim after 238 days was therefore barred, since a counter-claim is treated as a cross-suit for this purpose.
why_it_matters: Plaintiffs in commercial suits who face a counter-claim must treat the 120-day deadline for their reply with the same rigidity as a defendant's original written statement - there is no separate, more lenient timeline just because they are the original plaintiff.

case_name: Rohit Garg v. Union of India
holding_summary: The Delhi High Court held that the amended pre-deposit requirement under Section 107(6) of the CGST Act, effective from 1 October 2025, does not apply to appeals arising from show cause notices issued before that date, since the right of appeal is a substantive, vested right that accrues on the date proceedings are initiated (the SCN), not on the date the appeal is filed. The ruling arose in a batch of matters including a DGGI investigation into alleged fake invoicing and fraudulent ITC in the iron and steel trading sector, involving an aggregate demand of about Rs. 227.72 crore in the lead case.
why_it_matters: Businesses facing GST demands from show cause notices issued before October 2025 should apply the older, more favourable pre-deposit regime when filing their appeal, even if the adjudication order itself was passed after the amendment took effect.

case_name: Roadway Solutions India Infra Limited v. National Highways Authority of India
holding_summary: Ruling on a Section 9 Arbitration Act petition challenging NHAI's Notice of Intention to Terminate an EPC contract for six-laning the Kagal-Satara section of NH-48, Justice Om Prakash Shukla held that the mere presence of a termination clause providing for termination on specified defaults, with a cure-and-representation mechanism, does not make the EPC contract an inherently 'determinable' contract under Section 14(d) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The Court dismissed the interim injunction application, finding no prima facie case, with the balance of convenience favouring NHAI and the public interest in the highway project continuing, while leaving all contentions open for the arbitral tribunal.
why_it_matters: Contractors seeking to restrain termination of government EPC/infrastructure contracts under Section 9 should not assume an injunction will follow just because the contract has a termination clause - courts will scrutinise whether NHAI actually followed the contractual cure-and-representation process before concluding no prima facie case exists.

case_name: M/S Premium Transmission Pvt. Limited v. The State of Maharashtra
holding_summary: The Supreme Court dismissed a manufacturer's challenge to the Maharashtra government's reference of a contract-labour dispute for adjudication, holding that an apprehended industrial dispute need not be preceded by a formal, written demand from the workers before the government can make a reference under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Court directed the Industrial Court to specifically frame and decide the issues of whether the contractual labour arrangement was a sham and who was the real principal employer, disposing of the reference within four months.
why_it_matters: Employers cannot defeat a contract-labour reference on the technical ground that workers never issued a prior written demand - disputes about sham contracting arrangements and the identity of the principal employer will go to trial before the Industrial Court/Tribunal on the merits.

case_name: PI Opportunities Fund-I and Others v. Nagaraj V. Mylandla and Sharada Mylandla
holding_summary: Enforcing a 2024 Singapore-seated SIAC award that had held the promoters of Financial Software and Systems Pvt. Ltd. jointly and severally liable to pay the investors' exit price under a 2014 shareholders' agreement, the Supreme Court applied the doctrine of 'transnational issue estoppel' to reject the award-debtors' attempt to relitigate factual and contractual issues under Section 48 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. The Court held that issues already conclusively decided by the courts at the seat (Singapore) cannot be reopened at the enforcement stage in India, absent a genuine Indian public-policy objection.
why_it_matters: Award-debtors resisting enforcement of a foreign award in India now face a materially narrower Section 48 defence - they cannot simply repackage merits arguments the seat court already rejected, which strengthens the finality of foreign arbitral awards for parties (including PE/VC investors) enforcing against Indian promoters.

case_name: British Motor Car Company (1939) Ltd. v. M/S Hindustan Commercial Bank Ltd. (since merged with Punjab National Bank) & Anr.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that when a tenant bank is amalgamated into another bank under a scheme framed by RBI under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the resulting vesting of tenancy rights in the transferee bank amounts to 'parting with possession' (a form of sub-letting/assignment) under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, where the landlord's written consent was never obtained. The Court restored an eviction decree against Punjab National Bank over commercial premises in Connaught Circus, New Delhi, originally let to Hindustan Commercial Bank in 1947, holding that a statutory amalgamation scheme framed under banking law cannot override the landlord's rights under rent-control legislation.
why_it_matters: Banks and other entities that acquire leased premises through a statutory merger or amalgamation cannot assume the transfer is automatically insulated from rent-control consequences - landlords retain the right to seek eviction for want of consent, which is significant for any bank, NBFC, or corporate group planning a merger involving leasehold premises.

case_name: State Bank of India & Ors. v. Manoj Kumar Das & Ors.
holding_summary: A three-judge Bench (CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana) declined to interfere with the NCLAT's 30 June 2026 order, which had affirmed NCLT Mumbai's direction that provident fund, gratuity and pension dues of former Jet Airways employees be paid in full and treated as falling outside the corporate debtor's liquidation estate. Lenders led by SBI had argued these dues should form part of the liquidation estate and be shared under the IBC waterfall unless a dedicated PF/gratuity fund existed at the commencement of liquidation. The Court found the lenders' points arguable but, given the peculiar facts of the case, declined to interfere, leaving the underlying legal questions open for a future case.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that employee provident fund, gratuity and pension dues can be treated as trust monies outside the liquidation waterfall even without a dedicated fund, which matters for resolution professionals, liquidators and secured lenders assessing recoveries in stressed-asset liquidations.

case_name: State of U.P. v. Jai Bir Singh
court: Supreme Court of India (Nine-Judge Constitution Bench)
holding_summary: A nine-judge Constitution Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant (with Justices B.V. Nagarathna, P.S. Narasimha, Dipankar Datta, Ujjal Bhuyan, Satish Chandra Sharma, Joymalya Bagchi, Alok Aradhe and Vipul M. Pancholi) revisited the 'triple test' for what constitutes an 'industry', laid down by the seven-judge bench in Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa (1978). The Bench held that the 1978 triple test continues to govern industrial disputes still pending under the now-repealed Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, while refining aspects of that test, but held the 1978 ruling will no longer serve as the governing precedent ('sheet anchor') for disputes arising under the successor Industrial Relations Code.
why_it_matters: Ends decades of uncertainty over which establishments -- hospitals, educational bodies, government welfare departments, clubs -- qualify as an 'industry' for labour-dispute purposes, and narrows the expansive 1978 test's reach for future disputes; employers historically exposed under Bangalore Water Supply should reassess their position under the new Industrial Relations Code regime.

case_name: Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Union of India
holding_summary: The Supreme Court quashed a penalty for delayed deposit of Foreign Travel Tax that had escalated from Rs. 12,000 in the original adjudication to Rs. 71,29,140 after the airline successfully appealed and secured a remand for de novo adjudication. Invoking the principle against 'reformatio in peius' -- that a litigant should not be placed in a worse position for having exercised a statutory right of appeal -- the Court held that mere delay in depositing tax already collected does not amount to 'failure to pay' attracting penalty under Section 38(3) of the Finance Act, 1979, and directed refund of any penalty already paid, with 9% annual interest.
why_it_matters: Confirms that an appellate or remand process cannot be used to dramatically enhance a penalty beyond what was originally imposed, and clarifies that delayed remittance of tax already collected is legally distinct from non-payment -- relevant to any indirect-tax dispute where a taxpayer faces penalty escalation on remand.

case_name: Hari Dutta Sharma v. State of U.P. & Ors.
holding_summary: The Supreme Court held that a financier's right of self-help repossession of a hypothecated vehicle cannot be exercised through force, deceit, or in breach of the loan agreement's terms, after Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company repossessed the appellant's commercial truck at 1 a.m. by breaking its steering lock without prior notice, following a loan default. The Court directed the financier to close the loan account, refund Rs. 4.5 lakh realised from the vehicle's sale with 6% annual interest, and pay Rs. 10 lakh compensation for mental agony and loss of livelihood, and separately directed RBI to ensure banks and NBFCs actually comply with its existing recovery and repossession guidelines, observing that those guidelines have 'existed only on paper'.
why_it_matters: Sharply raises the litigation and compensation exposure for banks and NBFCs (and their recovery agents) that repossess vehicles or other hypothecated assets without following RBI's fair-practice and due-process norms, and places RBI under a fresh judicial mandate to supervise actual compliance rather than merely issuing circulars.
